sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The **Bechuanaland Protectorate (BP)** was a protectorate established on **31 March 1885** by the United Kingdom in southern Africa. It became the independent **Republic of Botswana** on **30 September 1966**. The name "Bechuanaland" meant the country of the Bechuana (now written Batswana or Tswana).

The Bechuanaland Protectorate was unique among British colonial possessions in Africa. It was not a colony but a **protectorate**—a form of indirect rule in which the British Crown provided military protection and managed foreign affairs, while the indigenous Tswana chiefs retained substantial authority over internal governance, land allocation, justice, and local administration. This distinction would prove crucial in preserving Tswana political structures and ultimately facilitating a peaceful transition to independence.

The protectorate covered an enormous area of approximately **712,000 km² (275,000 sq mi)**—roughly the size of France and Germany combined—but with a population in 1924 of only **152,980 people**. This vast, sparsely populated territory stretched from the Molopo River in the south to the Zambezi River in the north, and from the Kalahari Desert in the west to the Limpopo River in the east.

sections.title: The Geopolitical Context: Why Britain Acted

subsections.title: The Scramble for Africa
subsections.content: The creation of the Bechuanaland Protectorate must be understood within the broader context of the **late 19th-century Scramble for Africa**. European powers were racing to claim African territories, and southern Africa was a particular focus of competition among the British, the Boers (of the Transvaal Republic), and the Germans (who had established a presence in South-West Africa, modern Namibia).

subsections.title: The Strategic Importance of Bechuanaland
subsections.content: **Cecil Rhodes**, the ambitious Prime Minister of the Cape Colony, saw Bechuanaland as **"the key to the interior of Africa"**. He desperately sought to keep **"the road northward"** free of interference from the Transvaal Republic and Germany. The "road northward" was the route to the mineral wealth of the interior—the gold of the Transvaal, the diamonds of Kimberley, and the potential riches of the Zambezi region. If the Boers or Germans controlled Bechuanaland, they could block British expansion into the interior.

subsections.title: The Boer States of Stellaland and Goshen
subsections.content:
The immediate trigger for British intervention was the establishment of two short-lived **Boer republics** in Tswana territory: **Stellaland** and **Goshen**. These were created by Boer trekkers and adventurers who had crossed into Bechuanaland, seizing land from Tswana communities and setting up independent states. The Transvaal Republic backed these states, and there were fears that they could form a corridor linking the Transvaal to German South-West Africa.

The British government, under pressure from imperialists like Rhodes and missionaries like John Mackenzie, accepted in **1884** the notion that **Bechuanaland was vital for British interests**.

subsections.title: The Military Intervention
subsections.content:
In **December 1884**, Major-General **Sir Charles Warren** was sent as HM Special Commissioner to command a **military expedition to Bechuanaland**. The expedition's objectives were to:
- Assert British sovereignty in the face of encroachments from Germany and the Transvaal
- Suppress the Boer states of Stellaland and Goshen

Warren's force consisted of **4,000 British and local troops** who headed north from Cape Town. The expedition was notable for employing the **first three observation balloons ever used by the British Army in the field**—a sign of the technological modernity of the imperial project.

subsections.title: The Confrontation with Paul Kruger
subsections.content: On **22 January 1885**, Warren met the Boer leader **Paul Kruger** (future President of the Transvaal Republic) at the **Modder River**. Kruger sought to bring the expedition to a halt, offering to take responsibility for maintaining order in the Tswana country. Warren refused to abandon his march.

subsections.title: The Proclamation of the Protectorate
subsections.content: Upon reaching the area, Warren dissolved the republics of Stellaland and Goshen **without bloodshed**, and in **March 1885** announced the establishment of a British protectorate. In **September 1885**, he halved the size of the protectorate by proclaiming the Crown Colony of **British Bechuanaland** to the south (which was later annexed to the Cape Colony), while the northern portion became the **Bechuanaland Protectorate**. The border between the two followed the **Molopo and Nossob rivers**.

sections.title: The Tswana Chiefs and the Protectorate

subsections.title: The Three Paramount Chiefs
subsections.content:
The protectorate brought together **eight Tswana ethnic groups** of varying size, along with smaller Bantu groups such as the Wayeyi, Hambukushu, and Baherero, and hunter-gatherer communities collectively called the San, Basarwa, or Bushmen. The most powerful among them were the three paramount chiefs:

| Chief | Tribe | Region |
|-------|-------|--------|
| **Khama III** | Bangwato | Central Botswana (Serowe) |
| **Sebele I** | Bakwena | Southeastern Botswana (Molepolole) |
| **Bathoen I** | Bangwaketse | Southern Botswana (Kanye) |

These three chiefs are **credited with saving the young British Bechuanaland Protectorate from being absorbed by expansionist forces in the 1890s**.

subsections.title: Khama III's Support
subsections.content: **Khama III** (also known as "Khama the Great") **acquiesced happily** when Bechuanaland was declared a protectorate of Great Britain. He used British support to define and expand his northern territories. Khama saw the protectorate as a guarantee against Boer encroachment and Ndebele raids—a shield that would allow his kingdom to develop in peace.

subsections.title: The 1895 London Delegation
subsections.content:
In **1895**, the three chiefs—**Khama, Sebele, and Bathoen**—traveled to **London** to protest against the proposed annexation of their land in the Bechuanaland Protectorate by **Cecil Rhodes' British South Africa Company (BSAC)**. This was a remarkable journey: three African rulers traveling to the heart of the British Empire to plead their case directly to the Queen's government. Their delegation was successful—the annexation was blocked, and the protectorate remained under direct British control rather than being handed over to Rhodes' commercial enterprise.

The chiefs' successful lobbying in London demonstrated their political sophistication and their understanding of how to navigate the imperial system to protect their interests.

subsections.title: The Commissioner System
subsections.content:
The protectorate was administered by a series of British commissioners, whose titles changed over time:

| Period | Title |
|--------|-------|
| 1885–1891 | Deputy Commissioner |
| 1891–1964 | Resident Commissioner |
| 1964–1966 | Queen's Commissioner |

The first commissioner was **John Mackenzie** (1884–1885), the missionary who had long campaigned for British intervention. The last commissioner was **Hugh Norman-Walker** (1965–1966).

The Resident Commissioner was stationed at the administrative capital, **Mafeking** (now in South Africa), and acted under the authority of the **High Commissioner of South Africa**. The capital remained at Mafeking from **1885 to 1965**, when it was moved to **Gaborone** in preparation for independence.

subsections.title: The Kgotla System and Indirect Rule
subsections.content:
One of the defining features of the Bechuanaland Protectorate was the British commitment to **indirect rule** through the existing Tswana political structures. The British recognised that the **kgotla** (tribal council) system was an effective and legitimate form of governance.

**Key features of indirect rule in the Protectorate**:
- **Chiefs retained authority** over their own people in internal matters
- **The kgotla continued** to serve as the primary forum for dispute resolution and decision-making
- **Customary law** remained in force for most civil and criminal matters among Tswana subjects
- **Land allocation** remained under the authority of the chiefs
- The British **did not interfere** in succession disputes (except when they threatened stability)

However, the system was not without tensions. Indirect rule in Bechuanaland operated **differently from other parts of British Africa** because of the Tswana tradition of consultation and succession through primogeniture. The chiefs were not simply British puppets—they were genuine rulers who exercised real authority, and the British had to negotiate with them, not simply command them.

subsections.title: The Structure of Tswana Governance
subsections.content:
The traditional Tswana kingdoms had a hierarchical structure:
- Each section, district, community, village, ward, and family group were **independent of the rest** in managing their own affairs
- The **chief in kgotla** was the central authority—a representative gathering of all the males of the tribe
- This system was **"rather unwieldy"** for shouldering the increasing responsibilities of local government under colonial rule

subsections.title: Taxes and Revenue
subsections.content: The colonial administration imposed a **hut-tax** on the African population. This tax was a source of revenue for the protectorate and also served to encourage African men to seek wage labour, as they needed cash to pay the tax. The tax system created tensions and was a source of grievance among the population.

sections.title: The Threat of Annexation by South Africa

subsections.title: The Transfer Question
subsections.content:
Throughout the existence of the Bechuanaland Protectorate, there was a persistent threat that it would be **transferred to or annexed by South Africa**. This was known as the "Transfer Question" or "Annexation Question."

The Union of South Africa, established in 1910, saw the three British High Commission Territories—**Basutoland (Lesotho), Bechuanaland, and Swaziland**—as territories that should rightfully be part of the Union.

subsections.title: South African Pressure
subsections.content: In **1949**, South African Prime Minister **D.F. Malan** announced that he would seek the transfer of the three protectorates to the Union of South Africa. Observers believed that such a move would raise "every political and racial issue now latent in this subcontinent". The African populations of the protectorates, led by their chiefs and emerging political leaders, **vigorously opposed** incorporation into apartheid South Africa.

subsections.title: British Refusal
subsections.content:
The British government consistently refused to transfer the protectorates to South Africa. The reasons included:
- The strong opposition of the African populations
- The moral repugnance of handing African peoples over to the apartheid regime
- The strategic importance of the protectorates to British interests
- The lobbying efforts of missionaries and humanitarians in Britain

The refusal to transfer the protectorates to South Africa was one of the few bright spots in Britain's otherwise dismal record on decolonisation. It saved Botswana from the horrors of apartheid.

subsections.title: The Bechuanaland Democratic Party
subsections.content:
The movement toward independence was led by the **Bechuanaland Democratic Party (BDP)** , established in **1960** under the leadership of **Seretse Khama**.

**Seretse Khama** (1921–1980) was the grandson of Khama III and the rightful heir to the Bangwato chieftainship. He had been educated at Oxford University in England, where he met and married **Ruth Williams**, a white Englishwoman. This interracial marriage caused a scandal in both Britain and South Africa. The British government, under pressure from South Africa (which was then instituting apartheid), **banned Seretse from returning to the protectorate** for several years.

However, Seretse returned in **1956** with **popular support**, and he emerged as the leader of the independence movement. His blend of traditional legitimacy (as a royal heir), Western education, and democratic values made him the ideal leader for the transition to independence.

subsections.title: Self-Government and Independence
subsections.content:
- **1965**: The protectorate attained **self-government**
- **1 March 1965**: Seretse Khama became **Prime Minister**
- **30 September 1966**: Bechuanaland was granted independence and became the **Republic of Botswana**, with Seretse Khama as its **first President**

sections.title: Key Statistics and Facts
sections.content:
| Fact | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Establishment** | 31 March 1885 |
| **Area** | 712,000 km² (275,000 sq mi) |
| **Population (1924)** | 152,980 |
| **Capital (1885–1965)** | Mafeking (Mafikeng) |
| **Capital (1965–1966)** | Gaborone |
| **Official Language** | English |
| **Common Languages** | Setswana, IKalanga |
| **Currency (1885–1961)** | Pound sterling |
| **Currency (1961–1966)** | South African rand |
| **Independence** | 30 September 1966 |
| **First President** | Sir Seretse Khama |

subsections.title: Preservation of Tswana Political Structures
subsections.content: The most important legacy of the protectorate was the **preservation of Tswana political structures**. Unlike colonies where indigenous rulers were deposed or reduced to figureheads, the Tswana chiefs in the Bechuanaland Protectorate retained genuine authority over their people. When independence came, Botswana inherited a functioning system of traditional governance that complemented modern democratic institutions.

subsections.title: The Kgotla in Modern Botswana
subsections.content: The **kgotla system** remains a vital institution in Botswana today. Traditional courts operate alongside the modern judicial system, and chiefs continue to play a role in land allocation, customary law, and community leadership. The kgotla is also a symbol of Botswana's democratic tradition—a tradition of open debate and consensus-building that predates colonialism.

subsections.title: Avoidance of Apartheid
subsections.content: By refusing to transfer the protectorate to South Africa, Britain saved Botswana from incorporation into the apartheid system. This allowed Botswana to develop as a non-racial democracy, free from the racial oppression that afflicted its southern neighbour. Botswana's peaceful, democratic development stands in stark contrast to the violence and oppression that characterised apartheid South Africa.

subsections.title: Economic Foundations
subsections.content: The protectorate period laid some foundations for economic development, though Botswana was one of the poorest countries in the world at independence. The discovery of diamonds at **Orapa in 1967**—just one year after independence—would transform the country's fortunes. But the political stability and good governance established during the protectorate period created the conditions for this economic miracle.

subsections.title: A Model of Peaceful Decolonisation
subsections.content: Botswana's transition from protectorate to independent republic was **peaceful, orderly, and consensual**. There was no war of liberation, no violent struggle, no bitter conflict. This peaceful transition was a testament to the vision of leaders like Seretse Khama, the wisdom of the Tswana chiefs, and the pragmatic approach of the British colonial administration.

sections.title: Timeline of the Bechuanaland Protectorate
sections.content:
| Year | Event |
|------|-------|
| **1884** | British government accepts that Bechuanaland is vital for British interests |
| **December 1884** | Warren Expedition begins |
| **31 March 1885** | Bechuanaland Protectorate established |
| **September 1885** | Division into British Bechuanaland (south) and Bechuanaland Protectorate (north) |
| **1890** | Protectorate expanded northwards |
| **1895** | Khama, Sebele, and Bathoen travel to London to protest annexation |
| **1960** | Bechuanaland Democratic Party established under Seretse Khama |
| **1965** | Self-government attained |
| **1 March 1965** | Seretse Khama becomes Prime Minister |
| **30 September 1966** | Independence as Republic of Botswana |

keyFigures.name: Khama III
keyFigures.description: Khama III (also known as 'Khama the Great') acquiesced happily to the protectorate and used British support to define and expand his northern territories. He was a key figure in preserving the protectorate's integrity.

keyFigures.name: Sebele I
keyFigures.description: Sebele I was one of the three paramount chiefs who traveled to London in 1895 to protest annexation by the British South Africa Company, successfully blocking the move.

keyFigures.name: Bathoen I
keyFigures.description: Bathoen I was the third of the three chiefs who lobbied in London in 1895, demonstrating political sophistication in defending Tswana interests.

keyFigures.name: Seretse Khama
keyFigures.role: Leader of independence movement, first President of Botswana
keyFigures.description: Grandson of Khama III, educated at Oxford. Led the Bechuanaland Democratic Party, became Prime Minister in 1965, and President upon independence in 1966. His interracial marriage was controversial but he maintained popular support.

keyFigures.name: Cecil Rhodes
keyFigures.role: British imperialist, Prime Minister of Cape Colony
keyFigures.description: Saw Bechuanaland as 'the key to the interior of Africa' and sought to keep it free from Boer and German influence. His British South Africa Company tried to annex the protectorate in 1895 but was blocked.

keyFigures.name: John Mackenzie
keyFigures.role: Missionary, champion of African rights, first commissioner
keyFigures.description: Lived in Shoshong, advocated for British intervention to protect Tswana from Boers. Served as first Deputy Commissioner of the protectorate in 1884–1885.

keyFigures.name: Sir Charles Warren
keyFigures.description: Led the Warren Expedition in 1884–1885 to assert British sovereignty, suppress Boer republics, and establish the protectorate. Employed the first observation balloons used by the British Army.

keyFigures.name: Paul Kruger
keyFigures.role: Boer leader, later President of the Transvaal Republic
keyFigures.description: Met Warren at the Modder River in 1885 in an unsuccessful attempt to halt the expedition and maintain Boer control over Tswana territory.

keyFigures.name: D.F. Malan
keyFigures.description: Announced in 1949 that he would seek the transfer of the protectorates to South Africa, but faced vigorous opposition and British refusal.
